messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ramesh Patel is a 53-year-old married man who now makes his living as a house painter, though when he speaks about himself he does so with a quiet sense that the life he is in is not the one he was meant to be living. He grew up in a region marked by war and, during one bombardment in civilian housing, he was trapped in a collapsed building after an explosion tore through the street. What stays with him most is not a coherent sequence so much as fragments: the sharp chemical smell of smoke, dust, and burning material; the concussive bang that seemed to erase thought; and the helplessness of being pinned down, unable to control his body or protect the people beside him. He remembers being twisted awkwardly under debris, waiting for another strike, and the grief of realizing that not everyone nearby would come out alive. Even now, when he tries to tell the story, it can sound unreal to him, as if it happened to someone else, until his body suddenly tightens and he feels himself back in that position.

In the years since immigrating to the United States, Ramesh built a steady routine with his wife and found reliable work painting apartments and small commercial spaces. The trouble is that the very environment of his work brings him into contact with what he cannot manage. The smell of paint thinner, solvents, dust from sanding, or a faint burning odor in an old building can hit him with immediate force. A dropped ladder, a slammed dumpster lid, or the pop of construction equipment makes him jolt violently. Most difficult of all are moments when he cannot fully control what is happening around him—working on scaffolding while other crews move unpredictably, or being in a cramped room while someone else shuts the door. In those moments he becomes intensely watchful, scanning for exits, muscles drawn tight, body poised as if danger is seconds away. The trigger is never just a reminder; it convinces him afresh that the world is dangerous and that he is no longer a man who can function the way he once did.

When these reminders hit, memory does not come back as ordinary recollection. He feels his body curl and brace exactly as it had under the rubble, shoulders hunched and breath held, as if the scene is happening in the present. Along with that comes a wave of overwhelming grief, less about a single image than about the human loss embedded in the event. Because the memory arrives with such force, he has come to believe it says something final about him: that whatever competence and purpose once defined him are gone, and that nothing in his current life carries real meaning. Those thoughts make the memories harder to place in the past. He goes over and over why it happened to him, trying to find an answer that would make the suffering feel less arbitrary, but the rumination only keeps the event mentally active and close.

Over months and years, Ramesh has organized his life around not being caught by these states. He keeps relentlessly busy, taking extra jobs, staying in motion, filling evenings with tasks so there is little empty time in which his mind might drift back. He avoids news coverage of war, bombings, or civilian casualties because he knows even a brief report can leave him tense for hours. Yet the harder he works to push it away, the more sensitized he seems to become. Exhausted from constant effort and already on guard, he startles at ordinary sounds on the job and becomes more attentive to smells, enclosed spaces, and any hint that control is slipping. His wife has noticed that he no longer sits through televised reports with her and often paces the house afterward if loud noises come from outside. At work he has started turning down interior renovation jobs in crowded buildings, telling clients he is booked when in fact he is afraid of how quickly he can be thrown back into that bodily memory.

What frightens Ramesh most is how self-confirming it all feels. The more alert and tense his body becomes, the more easily a smell or bang grabs him; the more often he is jolted into the past, the more convinced he is that danger is everywhere and that he has been permanently diminished. He has come to watch himself closely for signs of losing control, and that vigilance itself makes those situations stand out all the more. By the time he sought help, the immediate reason was practical as much as emotional: after freezing and dropping his brush when a compressor backfired at a job site, he went home shaken and told his wife he could not keep pretending this was just stress. He says he wants “some peace” and to feel useful again, but underneath that hope is a fear that the war has followed him permanently, and that if he stops keeping busy for even a moment, the grief and the body memory will take over completely.
